name: engines-generators-and-fuels
description: Engines, Generators, and Fuel Sources: theory, design principles and practical build guidance for heat engines, power generators and every major fuel. The four laws of thermodynamics with the closed- and open-system energy balances and why enthalpy exists, entropy as energy unavailability rather than disorder, the Carnot ceiling and why raising T_H or lowering T_C is the only lever there has ever been — which makes engine efficiency a materials problem; working-fluid saturation, latent heat, the critical point, the classic misuse of the ideal gas law near saturation, and the specific-heat ratio. The Rankine cycle component by component, its back-work-ratio advantage, and the five improvements that carry real plants from 25-30% to 45-47% (superheat, reheat, regenerative feedwater heating, supercritical operation, and condensing at vacuum — with the worked 57% to 66% Carnot comparison behind Watt's separate condenser); reciprocating steam engines including cut-off and expansive working, compounding and uniflow, and steam turbines including impulse versus reaction, the Euler turbomachine equation, specific speed and blade tip-speed limits. The Otto cycle and knock as a fuel-chemistry rather than mechanical limit, volumetric efficiency, Atkinson/Miller and why hybrids use it; the Diesel cycle and why lean running forces DPF and SCR instead of a three-way catalyst; the Brayton cycle and its back-work-ratio problem; the Stirling engine and the four practical limits on its Carnot promise; and the combined cycle at 55-62%. Generators from Faraday's law through back-EMF, the four real loss mechanisms and the four machine types, AC versus DC generation and why inverter generators win at part load; then sizing, engine and generator-head selection, hybrid battery systems, transfer switching and the never-backfeed rule for a house power system. Every fuel with its energy density and the engine it pairs with — coal, petroleum fractions, natural gas, propane, wood and gasification, ethanol, biodiesel, biogas, hydrogen, uranium — plus nuclear, concentrated solar, PV, wind, hydro, geothermal and waste-heat ORC, HHV versus LHV, and combustion chemistry from stoichiometry to the equivalence ratio. Engine anatomy and the five-step rebuild, interference engines, ECU fuel trims as a diagnostic skill, forced induction, the materials table from crankshaft forging to single-crystal turbine blades, manufacturing process selection, and tolerance thinking including stack-up and GD&T. And the six things that kill: boiler explosions, carbon monoxide, electrical hazards, fuel fire, high-pressure steam and mechanical energy.
